# Financing, Incentives and Buydowns: Clark County New Construction

Research file for the Rose Homes LV new construction buyer guide.
Researcher: Financing, Incentive and Buydown Researcher.
All facts verified on 2026-07-25 unless noted otherwise.
Geography scope: Clark County, Nevada only. Pahrump, Mesquite and Boulder City are excluded. See the strip log at the bottom.

Citation format used throughout: `value [source: <URL> | verified: 2026-07-25]`.
Anything that could not be verified is written as `NOT FOUND`.

---

## 1. Loan limits for Clark County, NV (calendar year 2026)

### 1a. Conforming (Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac) limit

The 2026 baseline conforming loan limit for a one-unit home in most of the country is $832,750, an increase of $26,250 from 2025 [source: https://www.fhfa.gov/news/news-release/fhfa-announces-conforming-loan-limit-values-for-2026 | verified: 2026-07-25].

The 2026 high-cost ceiling for a one-unit home is $1,249,125, which is 150 percent of $832,750 [source: https://www.fhfa.gov/news/news-release/fhfa-announces-conforming-loan-limit-values-for-2026 | verified: 2026-07-25].

FHFA announced these values on November 25, 2025 [source: https://www.fhfa.gov/news/news-release/fhfa-announces-conforming-loan-limit-values-for-2026 | verified: 2026-07-25].

**Clark County is not a high-cost county.** Clark County uses the baseline. A one-unit conforming loan in Clark County in 2026 tops out at $832,750. Above that a buyer is in jumbo territory, which usually means a bigger down payment and tighter credit rules.

### 1b. FHA limit for Clark County

HUD set the 2026 FHA limits in Mortgagee Letter 2025-23, dated December 11, 2025, effective for FHA case numbers assigned on or after January 1, 2026 [source: https://www.hud.gov/sites/dfiles/hudclips/documents/2025-23hsgml.pdf | verified: 2026-07-25].

National FHA "floor" (low-cost area) limits for 2026, set at 65 percent of the $832,750 conforming limit [source: https://www.hud.gov/sites/dfiles/hudclips/documents/2025-23hsgml.pdf | verified: 2026-07-25]:

| Units | 2026 FHA floor |
|---|---|
| One | $541,287 |
| Two | $693,050 |
| Three | $837,700 |
| Four | $1,041,125 |

National FHA "ceiling" (high-cost area) limits for 2026, set at 150 percent of $832,750: one-unit $1,249,125, two-unit $1,599,375, three-unit $1,933,200, four-unit $2,402,625 [source: https://www.hud.gov/sites/dfiles/hudclips/documents/2025-23hsgml.pdf | verified: 2026-07-25].

**Clark County actual CY2026 FHA Forward limits**, pulled directly from HUD's official county lookup tool (Las Vegas-Henderson-North Las Vegas MSA, MSA code 29820, county code 003, last revised 01/01/2026) [source: https://entp.hud.gov/idapp/html/hicostlook.cfm | verified: 2026-07-25]:

| Units | Clark County CY2026 FHA limit |
|---|---|
| One | $541,287 |
| Two | $693,050 |
| Three | $837,700 |
| Four | $1,041,125 |

Median sale price HUD used for the Clark County determination: $462,000 [source: https://entp.hud.gov/idapp/html/hicostlook.cfm | verified: 2026-07-25].

**Clark County sits exactly at the national FHA floor.** That is because FHA sets the county limit at 115 percent of the area median price when that number falls between the floor and the ceiling [source: https://www.hud.gov/sites/dfiles/hudclips/documents/2025-23hsgml.pdf | verified: 2026-07-25]. For Clark County, 115 percent of $462,000 is below $541,287, so the floor applies.

> **Accuracy warning for the writing team.** Several third-party sites (LendingTree, fha.com and similar) were showing a Clark County 2026 FHA one-unit limit of $552,000 as of 2026-07-25. That number does not match HUD's own lookup tool, which returns $541,287. **Use $541,287.** Do not repeat the $552,000 figure.

### 1c. VA entitlement

VA does not apply a loan limit to a buyer with full entitlement. VA states that with full entitlement you "don't have a loan limit (as long as you can afford the loan amount and the property appraisal supports the purchase price of the home)" [source: https://www.va.gov/housing-assistance/home-loans/loan-limits/ | verified: 2026-07-25].

Key VA entitlement facts [source: https://www.va.gov/housing-assistance/home-loans/loan-limits/ | verified: 2026-07-25]:

- Basic entitlement applies to loans of $144,000 or less. Bonus entitlement covers amounts above that.
- A Certificate of Eligibility showing basic entitlement of $36,000 indicates full entitlement.
- With full entitlement, the VA guaranty "allows you to buy a home with no down payment."
- With partial or remaining entitlement, remaining bonus entitlement equals 25 percent of the county loan limit minus the entitlement already used, and the lender may require a down payment if remaining entitlement does not cover 25 percent of the loan.
- Full entitlement is not loan approval. The lender still underwrites credit, income, debts and assets.

VA funding fee amounts for 2026: NOT FOUND in this pass. Verify at https://www.va.gov before publishing any funding fee number.

## 2. Down payment assistance available in Clark County

Everything in this section is subject to change without notice. Every program below should be re-verified with the Nevada Housing Division or the specific agency before a buyer relies on it.

### 2a. Nevada Housing Division: Home Is Possible (HIP) For First-Time Homebuyers

The state's first-time buyer version of Home Is Possible [source: https://www.homeispossiblenv.org/home-possible-program | verified: 2026-07-25]:

- Down payment assistance up to 4 percent of the total loan amount, usable for down payment and closing costs.
- **Structure: "30 year non-forgivable."** This is a second lien that gets repaid. It is not a grant. The page describes it as "interest-free down-payment assistance."
- Must be a first-time homebuyer, defined as not having owned a home in the past 3 years.
- Minimum credit score 640 (660 for manufactured homes).
- Maximum debt ratio up to 50 percent, depending on credit score and loan type.
- Must occupy the home as a primary residence.
- Must complete a homebuyer education course.
- Statewide program.
- Maximum purchase price and income limits set by county for government loans.

**Clark County income and purchase price limits for the first-time buyer program**, as published by Nevada Housing Division and labeled "active as of June 15, 2026" [source: https://www.homeispossiblenv.org/page/first-time-homebuyer-income-purchase-price-limits | verified: 2026-07-25]:

| Item | Clark County limit |
|---|---|
| Maximum home purchase price | $566,354 |
| Maximum household income, 2 or fewer people | $105,500 |
| Maximum household income, 3 or more people | $121,325 |

The page adds an asterisk note: "Certain areas within this county may have a higher income limit. See lender for details." [source: https://www.homeispossiblenv.org/page/first-time-homebuyer-income-purchase-price-limits | verified: 2026-07-25]

### 2b. Nevada Housing Division: Home Is Possible (the non-first-time version)

A separate, more generous version with no first-time buyer requirement [source: https://www.homeispossiblenv.org/home-possible | verified: 2026-07-25]:

- Up to 5 percent of the loan value toward down payment or closing costs.
- Qualifying income up to $165,000.
- Home price up to $832,750 (this matches the 2026 conforming limit).
- Minimum credit score 640 (660 for manufactured homes).
- Maximum debt ratio for government loans (FHA, USDA, VA): 50 percent with a 680 or higher credit score, 45 percent below 680, 45 percent for manufactured homes. For conventional loans: 50 percent with 640 or higher.
- No first-time homebuyer requirement.
- The buyer may own one other property outside Nevada at time of close.
- Homebuyer education course required.
- Must live in the home as a primary residence.
- Available statewide, including manufactured homes.

**Grant or lien? NOT FOUND.** The current official Nevada Housing Division page for this program does not state whether the 5 percent is a grant, a forgivable loan or a repayable second lien [source: https://www.homeispossiblenv.org/home-possible | verified: 2026-07-25]. Older marketing material described HIP assistance as a grant, but that material also lists stale limits (income under $95,500, price under $400,000), so it cannot be relied on for 2026. **Do not describe the 5 percent as "free money" or a "grant" in the guide.** Tell the reader to ask the lender in writing whether it is a lien, and if so, what the term and payoff conditions are.

### 2c. Nevada Housing Division: Worker Advantage

This is the newest and, for many Las Vegas buyers, the most useful program. It launched December 10, 2025 [source: https://www.business.nv.gov/news-media/press-releases/2025/housing/nevada-housing-division-launches-new-down-payment-assistance-program-to-help-essential-workers-become-homeowners/ | verified: 2026-07-25].

Program details [source: https://www.homeispossiblenv.org/worker-advantage | verified: 2026-07-25]:

- **$20,000 in down payment assistance, "in the form of a no-interest, no-payment, non-forgivable 30-year second mortgage."** It is a lien, not a grant. It gets paid back.
- The buyer may apply the full amount to down payment, **or use it to reduce the interest rate on the first loan**, with anything left over going to down payment and closing costs. That buydown option matters a lot for new construction.
- Household income up to 150 percent of Area Median Income, which varies by county. The published statewide range runs from $101,550 in Mineral County to $175,250 in Storey and Washoe counties.
- Maximum purchase price $832,750.
- Minimum credit score 640 (660 for manufactured homes).
- Nevada residency for at least 6 months.
- Homebuyer education course required.
- No first-time homebuyer requirement.
- Must occupy as a primary residence.
- Cannot have previously used a Home Is Possible program.

**Clark County specific 150 percent AMI income cap for Worker Advantage: NOT FOUND.** The Nevada Housing Division page gives only the statewide range and does not publish a Clark County line item [source: https://www.homeispossiblenv.org/worker-advantage | verified: 2026-07-25]. Get the current Clark County number from a participating lender.

Eligible occupation categories are health care, education, public safety and construction trades [source: https://www.homeispossiblenv.org/worker-advantage | verified: 2026-07-25]. The official addendum lists specific job titles including physicians, RNs, LPNs, nurse practitioners, medical assistants, surgical technologists, radiologic technologists, lab technicians, pharmacists, home health aides, physical therapists, occupational therapists, medical receptionists, elementary/middle/high school teachers, special education teachers, school administrators, school counselors, school librarians, instructional coordinators, teacher aides, school secretaries, custodians and school bus drivers [source: https://www.homeispossiblenv.org/sites/default/files/2025-11/Worker%20Advantage%20Compliance%20Information.pdf | verified: 2026-07-25].

**Funding is finite and first-come, first-served.** The program is backed by $18 million under Governor Lombardo's Nevada Housing Access and Attainability Act, and "will remain open until all allocated funds have been reserved." The state estimated that would support roughly 900 households [source: https://www.business.nv.gov/news-media/press-releases/2025/housing/nevada-housing-division-launches-new-down-payment-assistance-program-to-help-essential-workers-become-homeowners/ | verified: 2026-07-25].

Reported uptake as of early January 2026: 81 of 900 slots used, roughly 819 remaining [source: https://www.fox5vegas.com/2026/01/08/nevadas-worker-advantage-program-still-has-funding-available-essential-workers/ | verified: 2026-07-25]. **That figure is from January 2026 and is more than six months stale as of this writing.** The guide must not print a "spots remaining" number. Say the funding is limited and tell the reader to confirm current availability.

Processing note for the transaction timeline: the lender must send NHD the Nevada residency proof and the Verification of Employment at least 5 days prior to closing, and NHD emails a "Clear to Close" letter within 24 hours [source: https://www.homeispossiblenv.org/sites/default/files/2025-11/Worker%20Advantage%20Compliance%20Information.pdf | verified: 2026-07-25]. On a new build, that is a real scheduling item, because builder closing dates move.

**Conflict flag:** a third-party summary of the eHousingPlus administrator guide for Worker Advantage listed a purchase price limit of $806,500, which is the 2025 conforming limit, while the Nevada Housing Division page says $832,750. The administrator guide PDF could not be retrieved directly for verification. **Treat the purchase price limit as "confirm with the lender."**

### 2d. Nevada Housing Division: Home Is Possible For Teachers

[source: https://www.homeispossiblenv.org/home-possible-teachers | verified: 2026-07-25]

- $7,500 usable for down payment and closing costs.
- **Forgivable after five years if the buyer stays in the home.** This one really is forgivable, unlike the others.
- Licensed full-time K-12 public school classroom teachers employed in Nevada.
- No first-time homebuyer requirement.
- Qualifying income up to $165,000.
- Home price up to $832,750.
- Minimum credit score 640 (660 for manufactured homes).
- Maximum debt ratio 50 percent depending on credit score and loan type.
- Homebuyer education course required.
- **"This program is available through December 31, 2026."** This is a hard expiration date and the guide should say so.

### 2e. Clark County and city programs

**Clark County: Welcome Home Community Land Trust.** Clark County has been standing up a shared-equity community land trust for low to moderate income first-time buyers, where the trust owns the land and the homeowner owns the house. The county said it expected to roll the program out in late 2025 and open homebuyer applications in Q2 2026, and lists a 3 percent down payment for CLT homes such as the Rebecca Place development [source: https://www.clarkcountynv.gov/government/departments/community_housing_office/community_land_trust/homebuyer | verified: 2026-07-25]. Current application status as of 2026-07-25: NOT FOUND. Contact CCCLT@ClarkCountyNV.gov.

This is **not** a production-builder new construction program. Do not present it as a way to buy a Lennar or KB home.

Clark County's Affordable and Attainable Housing Trust Fund revenues "may be used for down-payment assistance, homeowner rehabilitation, and emergency rental assistance" [source: https://www.clarkcountynv.gov/residents/community_housing_fund/ | verified: 2026-07-25]. Whether any of that currently funds a direct-to-buyer DPA product: NOT FOUND.

**City of Las Vegas homebuyer DPA program:** NOT FOUND on an official city source in this pass.

**City of Henderson homebuyer DPA program:** NOT FOUND on an official city source in this pass. Secondary sources say Henderson does not currently administer a first-time homebuyer program. Not verified against cityofhenderson.com.

**City of North Las Vegas homebuyer DPA program:** NOT FOUND on an official city source in this pass. Secondary sources reference a past program and an amount of up to $14,999. **That number is unverified. Do not print it.**

**Nevada Rural Housing (Home At Last, Launchpad, Rural Rocks $20K):** these serve the 15 rural counties plus "the rural parts of Clark and Washoe counties," with parcel eligibility checked at HALMap.org [source: https://nvrural.org/programs/homeownership/down-payment-assistance/ | verified: 2026-07-25]. The rural parts of Clark County do **not** include Las Vegas, Henderson, North Las Vegas, Summerlin, Spring Valley, Enterprise, Paradise, Centennial Hills, Skye Canyon, Mountain's Edge, Inspirada or Cadence. For a Las Vegas valley new construction buyer these programs are almost certainly not available. Mention only in passing, or omit.

## 3. Rate buydowns, explained mechanically

This is the single most misunderstood thing in new construction. Everything below is sourced.

### 3a. Temporary buydown (the 2-1, the 3-2-1, the 1-0)

**What it is.** Somebody deposits a lump sum of cash into a separate account at closing. Each month, a slice of that account is released to top up the buyer's payment, so the buyer's out-of-pocket payment is smaller in the early years. The note rate never changes.

Fannie Mae describes the mechanic this way: the effective rate the borrower pays in the early years is reduced "as a result of the deposit of a lump sum of money (sometimes called a subsidy) into a buydown account, a portion of which is released each month to reduce the borrower's payments" [source: https://selling-guide.fanniemae.com/sel/b2-1.4-04/temporary-interest-rate-buydowns | verified: 2026-07-25].

**The rate on the note is never actually lowered.** The full note rate and the full payment are what the buyer legally owes, and that is what appears on the mortgage documents [source: https://selling-guide.fanniemae.com/sel/b2-1.4-04/temporary-interest-rate-buydowns | verified: 2026-07-25]. This is the sentence the guide has to land.

**Limits.** Fannie Mae allows increases "of not more than 1% in the portion of the interest rate paid by the borrower in each 1-year interval," a maximum total reduction of 3 percent, and a buydown period that cannot exceed 3 years [source: https://selling-guide.fanniemae.com/sel/b2-1.4-04/temporary-interest-rate-buydowns | verified: 2026-07-25]. VA describes the same 1 percent per year step-up and says temporary buydowns "typically last one to three years," with 3-2-1 and 2-1 being the common structures [source: https://www.benefits.va.gov/homeloans/temporary-buydown.asp | verified: 2026-07-25].

**The account is walled off.** Buydown funds must sit in a separate escrow account, protected from creditors of the lender, seller, builder or the buyer, and they cannot be used for anything else or returned to whoever funded the account [source: https://www.benefits.va.gov/homeloans/temporary-buydown.asp | verified: 2026-07-25]. Fannie Mae requires the funds be in custodial bank accounts, fully funded by the time the loan is delivered, and not commingled with the lender's corporate funds [source: https://selling-guide.fanniemae.com/sel/b2-1.4-04/temporary-interest-rate-buydowns | verified: 2026-07-25].

**The buyer must qualify at the real rate.** Fannie Mae: the lender "must qualify the borrower based on the note rate without consideration of the bought-down rate" [source: https://selling-guide.fanniemae.com/sel/b2-1.4-04/temporary-interest-rate-buydowns | verified: 2026-07-25]. VA: qualification must be based "on the full monthly payment amount that the borrower will owe after the temporary buydown period ends" [source: https://www.benefits.va.gov/homeloans/temporary-buydown.asp | verified: 2026-07-25]. So a 2-1 does not let a buyer buy more house. It only softens the first two years.

**What happens in year 3 of a 2-1.** Nothing gets renegotiated. The subsidy account is empty. The buyer's payment steps up to the full note payment and stays there for the remaining 28 years. Year 1 the buyer pays as if the rate were 2 points lower. Year 2, 1 point lower. Year 3 onward, the actual note rate. That is the whole product.

**What the buyer owns at the end of a 2-1: nothing.** The subsidy is spent. There is no equity created, no rate improvement retained, no residual. If the buyer sells or refinances early, VA requires that remaining funds in the buydown account "must be applied to the outstanding indebtedness" [source: https://www.benefits.va.gov/homeloans/temporary-buydown.asp | verified: 2026-07-25]. In other words the leftover money reduces the loan balance. It does not get handed back to the buyer as cash.

**Plain-language version for the guide:**
> A 2-1 buydown is a two-year discount on your payment, prepaid by somebody else and parked in a side account. Your real interest rate never changes. In year three the side account is empty and you pay the full payment. The full payment is the payment you should decide on.

### 3b. Permanent buydown (discount points)

**What it is.** The buyer, or the builder on the buyer's behalf, pays cash at closing to purchase a genuinely lower note rate that lasts the full life of the loan.

CFPB: "One point equals one percent of the loan amount. For example, one point on a $100,000 loan is one percent of the loan amount, which equals $1,000" [source: https://www.consumerfinance.gov/ask-cfpb/what-are-discount-points-and-lender-credits-and-how-do-they-work-en-136/ | verified: 2026-07-25].

CFPB: "Paying points lowers your interest rate, compared to the interest rate you could get with a zero-point loan at the same lender," and how much the rate drops "depends on the specific lender, the kind of loan, and the overall mortgage market" [source: https://www.consumerfinance.gov/ask-cfpb/what-are-discount-points-and-lender-credits-and-how-do-they-work-en-136/ | verified: 2026-07-25].

There is no fixed "1 point equals 0.25 percent" rule. That ratio moves daily. **Do not publish a points-to-rate conversion in the guide.**

**What the buyer owns at the end: a permanently lower note rate.** If the buyer keeps the loan long enough, a permanent buydown is worth more than a temporary one. If the buyer refinances or sells in two years, the money spent on points is gone.

CFPB's recommended way to decide: "ask a loan officer to show you two different options (with and without points or credits) and to calculate the total costs over a few different possible timeframes," specifically "the shortest amount of time, the longest amount of time, and the most likely amount of time you can see yourself keeping the loan" [source: https://www.consumerfinance.gov/ask-cfpb/what-are-discount-points-and-lender-credits-and-how-do-they-work-en-136/ | verified: 2026-07-25].

### 3c. Builder forward commitment

**What it is.** The builder pays a fee to a lender in advance to lock a below-market rate on a pool of future loans, then offers that rate only to buyers of its homes. It is a bulk pre-purchase of rate.

A forward commitment has been described as a builder's promise to deliver a set amount of loan volume to a lender, with the lender locking that volume at a predetermined rate in exchange for a fee from the builder [source: https://www.builderonline.com/money/mortgage-finance/how-forward-commitments-help-builders-win | verified: 2026-07-25]. A permanent buydown can be delivered through a "bulk forward commitment," where the builder pays a fee in advance to purchase a commitment on a large pool of mortgage money at a lower rate [source: https://acrisuremortgage.com/forward-commitments/ | verified: 2026-07-25].

**Why it matters to the buyer:**
- The advertised rate is real and permanent, not a two-year mirage, if it is structured as a permanent buydown.
- It is almost always tied to the builder's own lender, because the builder bought the commitment through that lender.
- Forward commitments are usually attached to **specific inventory**, most often standing spec homes the builder wants gone, and often with a hard close-by date. Ask which homes qualify and by when.
- These programs have expiration dates and can be pulled. Verify the offer in writing.

Current live Las Vegas builder forward commitment rates and terms as of 2026-07-25: NOT FOUND. These change weekly by builder and by community. The guide should teach the reader to ask, not print a number.

### 3d. Who is allowed to pay for a buydown, and how much

Buydown money is a seller or interested-party contribution and is subject to concession caps.

**Conventional (Fannie Mae)** interested party contribution limits for a principal residence or second home [source: https://selling-guide.fanniemae.com/sel/b3-4.1-02/interested-party-contributions-ipcs | verified: 2026-07-25, guide dated May 7, 2025]:

| LTV / CLTV | Max IPC |
|---|---|
| Greater than 90 percent | 3 percent |
| 75.01 percent to 90 percent | 6 percent |
| 75 percent or less | 9 percent |
| Investment property, any LTV | 2 percent |

Also from that section [source: https://selling-guide.fanniemae.com/sel/b3-4.1-02/interested-party-contributions-ipcs | verified: 2026-07-25]:
- IPCs may pay borrower closing costs including prepaids, and HOA assessments limited to 12 months after settlement.
- "Fannie Mae does not permit IPCs to be used to make the borrower's down payment, meet financial reserve requirements, or meet minimum borrower contribution requirements."
- **Temporary and permanent interest rate buydowns funded by interested parties count toward the IPC limit.** This is why a builder cannot stack an unlimited buydown on top of unlimited closing cost help.

**VA:** a builder-funded or seller-funded temporary buydown counts as a seller concession, "capped at 4% of the reasonable value" [source: https://www.benefits.va.gov/homeloans/temporary-buydown.asp | verified: 2026-07-25].

**FHA:** the commonly applied limit on interested party contributions is 6 percent of the sales price, per HUD Handbook 4000.1. **NOT VERIFIED against a primary HUD source in this pass** (the HUD FAQ page renders through JavaScript and could not be read; the only HUD-hosted text found quoting "six (6) percent" was Mortgagee Letter 2005-02, which is too old to cite as current). Confirm the current FHA figure with the lender before publishing it. Handbook location: https://www.hud.gov/hud-partners/single-family-lender

**Checked for 2026 changes:** HUD Mortgagee Letter 2026-06, dated June 23, 2026, concerns the maximum number of draw requests under the Limited 203(k) rehabilitation program and does not touch seller concessions [source: https://www.hud.gov/sites/default/files/hudclips/documents/2026-06hsgml.pdf | verified: 2026-07-25].

## 4. The in-house lender question

### 4a. What actually happens

Most large production builders own or are affiliated with a mortgage company and a title company. The builder's incentive, whether it is a rate buydown, closing cost credit or design center credit, is usually conditioned on the buyer financing through that affiliated lender.

### 4b. Why that is legal

RESPA prohibits "required use" of a particular settlement service provider, but the definition of required use carves out optional discount packages. The regulation says:

> "Required use means a situation in which a person must use a particular provider of a settlement service in order to have access to some distinct service or property, and the person will pay for the settlement service of the particular provider or will pay a charge attributable, in whole or in part, to the settlement service. However, the offering of a package (or combination of settlement services) or the offering of discounts or rebates to consumers for the purchase of multiple settlement services does not constitute a required use. Any package or discount must be optional to the purchaser. The discount must be a true discount below the prices that are otherwise generally available, and must not be made up by higher costs elsewhere in the settlement process."
>
> [source: https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/12/1024.2 | verified: 2026-07-25, 12 CFR 1024.2(b)]

So a builder may lawfully offer a bigger incentive for using its lender, provided the buyer can still buy the home without using that lender, the discount is a genuine discount, and the builder does not claw it back through inflated costs elsewhere in the deal. Those last two conditions are exactly what an honest comparison tests.

### 4c. The affiliated business arrangement disclosure

When a settlement service provider refers business to an affiliate, RESPA requires a written disclosure. 12 CFR 1024.15 requires a "written disclosure, in the format of the Affiliated Business Arrangement Disclosure Statement set forth in appendix D" explaining "the nature of the relationship" and giving "an estimated charge or range of charges" [source: https://www.consumerfinance.gov/rules-policy/regulations/1024/15/ | verified: 2026-07-25].

Timing: the disclosure must be provided "no later than the time of each referral or, if the lender requires use of a particular provider, the time of loan application" [source: https://www.consumerfinance.gov/rules-policy/regulations/1024/15/ | verified: 2026-07-25].

The safe harbor also requires that "no person making a referral has required (as defined in § 1024.2, 'required use') any person to use any particular provider of settlement services," with narrow exceptions, such as a lender requiring an attorney, credit reporting agency or appraiser of the lender's choosing [source: https://www.consumerfinance.gov/rules-policy/regulations/1024/15/ | verified: 2026-07-25].

**Practical takeaway for the guide.** The buyer should receive an Affiliated Business Arrangement Disclosure Statement, usually at the sales office at the time of the referral. It names the relationship and gives a range of charges. It is a real document, and reading it is free.

### 4d. The exact comparison procedure

This is the section the guide most needs. Give the reader these steps in this order.

**Step 1. Get a Loan Estimate from the builder's lender.**
A lender must provide a Loan Estimate "within three business days of receiving your application" [source: https://www.consumerfinance.gov/ask-cfpb/when-will-i-receive-my-loan-estimate-en-1995/ | verified: 2026-07-25]. Apply with the builder's lender and get the document. Do not accept a "worksheet," a "fee sheet," a "scenario" or a screenshot. Ask for the Loan Estimate.

**Step 2. Get at least one outside Loan Estimate for the same loan, same day.**
CFPB: "the best way to tell if you have a competitive loan offer is to compare it to Loan Estimates from other lenders," and the estimates should be for identical loan types [source: https://www.consumerfinance.gov/owning-a-home/loan-estimate/ | verified: 2026-07-25]. Same loan type, same loan amount, same down payment, same lock period, same day. Rates move daily, so a Loan Estimate from Tuesday cannot be compared to one from the following Monday.

**Step 3. Write the builder incentive down as a dollar amount.**
Get it in writing from the sales office: exactly how many dollars, tied to what, and expiring when. If part of it is a buydown, ask for the dollar cost of the buydown, not the advertised rate.

**Step 4. Compare on page 3, not page 1.**
Every Loan Estimate has a "Comparisons" section on page 3 with three numbers: the total you will have paid in principal, interest, mortgage insurance and loan costs "In 5 Years," the APR, and the Total Interest Percentage (TIP) [source: https://www.consumerfinance.gov/owning-a-home/loan-estimate/ | verified: 2026-07-25]. Use the "In 5 Years" number as the anchor, because most buyers do not keep a mortgage 30 years.

**Step 5. Do the arithmetic over the years the buyer actually expects to stay.**

For each lender:

```
Total cost over N years
  = (monthly payment in each year x 12, summed over N years)
  + all closing costs the buyer pays
  - any credit or incentive the buyer receives
  - any remaining principal reduction difference
```

Simplified and usable version for the guide:

```
Builder lender:   [In 5 Years figure from page 3]  -  [builder incentive in dollars]  =  A
Outside lender:   [In 5 Years figure from page 3]  -  [any credit from that lender]   =  B

If A is smaller, the builder lender wins. If B is smaller, it does not.
```

If the buyer expects to stay 3 years or 10 years instead of 5, ask both loan officers for the same total-cost figure at that horizon. CFPB explicitly suggests running "the shortest amount of time, the longest amount of time, and the most likely amount of time" [source: https://www.consumerfinance.gov/ask-cfpb/what-are-discount-points-and-lender-credits-and-how-do-they-work-en-136/ | verified: 2026-07-25].

**Step 6. Check for the claw-back.**
Compare Section A (Origination Charges), Section B (Services You Cannot Shop For) and Section C (Services You Can Shop For) side by side. RESPA's own standard is that the discount "must not be made up by higher costs elsewhere in the settlement process" [source: https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/12/1024.2 | verified: 2026-07-25]. If the builder lender's incentive is $15,000 but its origination and title charges are $6,000 higher, the real incentive is $9,000.

**Step 7. Ask the two questions in writing.**
1. If I use an outside lender, what exactly do I lose? Get the dollar figure.
2. Is any part of this incentive contingent on also using the builder's title or escrow company?

**A note the guide should include:** a buyer can shop the loan and still take the builder's lender. Getting a second Loan Estimate does not obligate anyone. It is the only way to know whether the incentive is real.

---

## 5. Closing cost reality on a Clark County new build

### 5a. Nevada is an escrow state

Nevada closes through a neutral third party, not through an attorney-conducted settlement. Escrow is defined by statute in NRS Chapter 645A, and NRS 692A.240 allows a person to administer escrows if licensed as a title insurer, title agent or escrow officer under Title 57, or as an escrow agent or escrow agency under NRS 645A [source: https://www.leg.state.nv.us/nrs/NRS-645A.html | verified: 2026-07-25].

The Nevada Division of Insurance regulates both: NRS 692A covers title insurance and NRS 645A covers escrow agent and agency licensing. A person working for a title agent or insurer "can be licensed as an escrow officer if they only handle escrows and do not sell, solicit, or negotiate insurance," while someone not employed by a title entity "can be licensed as an escrow agent (natural person) or escrow agency (firm)" [source: https://doi.nv.gov/Licensing/License_Types/Title_and_Escrow/ | verified: 2026-07-25].

In practice in Las Vegas, the escrow officer sits inside a title company. On a builder purchase, the builder normally names the title and escrow company, and that company is frequently a builder affiliate. The same affiliated business arrangement disclosure rules in Section 4c apply.

### 5b. What the buyer pays

Buyer-side charges on a Clark County new build fall into these buckets. The guide should list the buckets and tell the reader the actual dollars come from the Loan Estimate and the builder's purchase agreement, not from a guide.

- Lender charges: origination, discount points if any, credit report, appraisal.
- Prepaids: prepaid interest to the end of the closing month, first-year homeowners insurance premium, initial escrow/impound deposits for taxes and insurance.
- Title and escrow: lender's title policy premium, escrow fee split, recording fees.
- Any first installment or proration of an SID or LID assessment (see Section 7).
- HOA: transfer/setup fee, first month or first quarter of dues, and in a master-planned community often a one-time community enhancement or transfer fee.

Typical dollar ranges for Clark County new construction closing costs as of 2026-07-25: NOT FOUND from any authoritative source. Do not print a range. Print the checklist and tell the reader to get the Loan Estimate and the builder's estimated closing statement.

### 5c. What the builder typically pays

**Customary allocation on a Clark County new build: NOT FOUND from an authoritative source.** Builder closing cost contributions are negotiated deal by deal and are almost always conditioned on using the affiliated lender and title company. Anything more specific would be fabrication.

What the guide can safely say: builder closing cost credits are subject to the same interested-party contribution caps in Section 3d, they usually cannot be used for the down payment, and the buyer should get the number in writing before signing.

### 5d. Title insurance in Nevada

One general Nevada custom, from a secondary source and flagged as such: "It is common for the seller to pay for the buyer's policy of title insurance and for the buyer to pay for its own lender's policy of title insurance as well as any costs associated with obtaining or recording a new loan" [source: https://nvbar.org/wp-content/uploads/SBN-Public-Info-Brochure-Real-Estate-fn.pdf | verified: 2026-07-25, State Bar of Nevada consumer brochure]. **Whether a specific builder follows this custom: NOT FOUND.** Builder contracts override custom. Read the contract.

### 5e. Real Property Transfer Tax

Clark County collects real property transfer tax at recording under NRS Chapter 375. The rate is $2.55 per $500 of value or fraction thereof, based on the full purchase price or the estimated fair market value, and buyer and seller are jointly and severally liable for any additional amount owed [source: https://webfiles.clarkcountynv.gov/Recorder/Forms/RPTT_Supporting_Documentation_Brochure.pdf | verified: 2026-07-25]. Statute: https://www.leg.state.nv.us/nrs/NRS-375.html

On a $500,000 new build that is 1,000 increments of $500, so $2,550 of transfer tax. Who pays it on a builder contract: **NOT FOUND**, it is contract-specific. Check the purchase agreement.

## 6. Property tax math for Clark County

This section contains the single biggest new-construction money surprise in the valley. Get it right.

### 6a. How the number is built

Nevada does not tax market value directly. The chain is:

1. **Taxable value.** The Assessor uses a cost approach: "replacement cost of the improvement less depreciation and market value of the land." A depreciation factor of 1.5 percent per year applies, capped at 50 years. Improvement replacement costs are updated annually using the Marshall & Swift Building Cost Service [source: https://www.clarkcountynv.gov/government/assessor/real-property | verified: 2026-07-25].
2. **Assessed value = taxable value x 0.35.** The assessment ratio is 35 percent. The Assessor's own example: a $200,000 taxable value gives a $70,000 assessed value [source: https://www.clarkcountynv.gov/government/assessor/real-property | verified: 2026-07-25].
3. **Tax = assessed value x tax rate per $100.** Assessor example: $70,000 assessed at a rate of 3.2782 per $100 produces $2,294.74 in annual tax [source: https://www.clarkcountynv.gov/government/assessor/real-property | verified: 2026-07-25].

**Actual FY 2026-2027 Clark County tax rates**, pulled from the Clark County Treasurer's rate-by-district tool [source: https://treasurer.co.clark.nv.us/TaxRate-District/ | verified: 2026-07-25]:

| Tax district | Area | FY2026-2027 total rate per $100 |
|---|---|---|
| 200 | Las Vegas City | 3.2782 |
| 250 | North Las Vegas City | 3.3544 |
| 505 | Henderson Artesian Basin | 2.9613 |
| 635 | Enterprise (fire, artesian, library, 911, manpower) | 2.9328 |
| 630 | Enterprise (artesian, library, manpower) | 2.7081 |
| 411 | Winchester CC Redevelopment | 2.9328 |

Rates vary by district within each city. A buyer must look up the actual district for the actual parcel. There are well over a hundred districts in Clark County.

Statutory ceiling: the Nevada Constitution caps total ad valorem property tax at $5.00 per $100 of assessed valuation, and NRS 361.453(1) further limits the combined rate to $3.64 per $100 [source: https://www.leg.state.nv.us/nrs/NRS-361.html | verified: 2026-07-25].

### 6b. The abatement (the "tax cap") and the catch

Nevada caps how fast a tax **bill** can rise, not how fast value can rise.

- **3 percent cap** on the tax bill of an owner's primary residence, whether a single-family house, townhouse, condominium or manufactured home, under NRS 361.4723. Only one property per person statewide may qualify as a primary residence [source: https://www.clarkcountynv.gov/government/general_information/tax-abatement | verified: 2026-07-25].
- **Up to 8 percent cap** on residences that are not owner occupied, and on land, commercial buildings, business personal property and similar [source: https://www.clarkcountynv.gov/government/general_information/tax-abatement | verified: 2026-07-25]. The statute sets the general cap at the lesser of 8 percent or the greater of (a) the 10-year average percentage change in county assessed valuation, (b) twice the increase in CPI for all Urban Consumers, U.S. City Average, for the preceding calendar year, or (c) zero [source: https://www.leg.state.nv.us/nrs/NRS-361.html | verified: 2026-07-25, NRS 361.4722(1)(b)].

**Catch #1: a brand new home gets NO cap in its first fiscal year.**

Clark County states it plainly: "New construction or property that has a change of use (zoning change or manufactured home conversion) will not qualify for any cap for this fiscal year but will receive the 3% or up to an 8% cap starting the following fiscal year" [source: https://www.clarkcountynv.gov/government/general_information/tax-abatement | verified: 2026-07-25].

The statute is why. Both cap sections apply only to property "for which an assessed valuation was separately established for the immediately preceding fiscal year," and both explicitly exclude "any increase in the assessed valuation of the property from the immediately preceding fiscal year as a result of any improvement to or change in the actual or authorized use of the property" [source: https://www.leg.state.nv.us/nrs/NRS-361.html | verified: 2026-07-25, NRS 361.4722(1) and NRS 361.4723(1) and (2)(a)]. A house that did not exist last year has no prior-year assessed value to cap against, and the house itself is "an improvement."

**Catch #2: recording the deed knocks the 3 percent cap off, and the new owner has to claim it back.**

Clark County: "Any ownership document recorded will remove your Owner Occupied 3% abatement." The Assessor mails postcards after July 1 to properties whose ownership or document number changed during that fiscal year, and the owner must sign and return the postcard "as soon as possible to retain the 3% tax cap" [source: https://www.clarkcountynv.gov/government/general_information/tax-abatement | verified: 2026-07-25].

**This is the one that burns new construction buyers.** They close, they move in, a postcard arrives from the Assessor months later, it looks like junk mail, they throw it away, and their bill jumps to the 8 percent cap instead of the 3 percent cap. The guide should tell the reader in plain words: watch for a postcard from the Clark County Assessor after July 1, sign it, send it back.

Falsely claiming the abatement carries a penalty of three times the tax deficiency, plus the tax and any other penalty [source: https://www.leg.state.nv.us/nrs/NRS-361.html | verified: 2026-07-25, NRS 361.4735]. So the claim is a real legal statement, not a formality.

### 6c. Why the first tax bill often looks like land only

The Assessor lists and values property "in the county on July 1" and assesses it to the July 1 owner [source: https://www.leg.state.nv.us/nrs/NRS-361.html | verified: 2026-07-25, NRS 361.260(1)]. If the house was not standing on the July 1 lien date, there is no improvement value to place on the secured roll for that fiscal year. The bill reflects the lot.

NRS 361.260(3) covers the near-miss case: "An improvement on real property in existence on July 1 whose existence was not ascertained in time to be placed on the secured roll for that tax year and which is not governed by subsection 4 must be placed on the unsecured tax roll" [source: https://www.leg.state.nv.us/nrs/NRS-361.html | verified: 2026-07-25].

**What this means for the buyer.** The first-year tax bill, and therefore the first-year escrow/impound calculation, can be based on a fraction of the eventual tax. The following year the house appears on the roll, the bill roughly triples or more, the escrow account comes up short, and the monthly payment jumps for two reasons at once: the shortage repayment and the higher ongoing tax. Combine that with a 2-1 buydown expiring and you can have a very ugly year 2 or year 3.

**The guide must connect these two things.** Tell the reader to ask the lender to escrow based on the fully-assessed tax on a completed home, not on the land-only bill.

### 6d. Billing and due dates

Property tax bills are mailed once per fiscal year, and the Treasurer advises contacting them if a bill is not received by August 1 [source: https://www.clarkcountynv.gov/government/elected_officials/county_treasurer/real-property-tax-information | verified: 2026-07-25].

Taxes are due the third Monday of August, and may be paid in four approximately equal installments if the taxes on the parcel exceed $100 [source: https://www.leg.state.nv.us/nrs/NRS-361.html | verified: 2026-07-25, NRS 361.483].

The four Clark County installment due dates [source: https://www.clarkcountynv.gov/government/elected_officials/county_treasurer/real-property-tax-information | verified: 2026-07-25]:

1. 3rd Monday in August
2. 1st Monday in October
3. 1st Monday in January
4. 1st Monday in March

Payments must be made within 10 days of the due date to avoid penalty. Penalties escalate with the number of delinquent installments, from 4 percent for a single missed installment up to 22 percent on the first installment when all four are delinquent [source: https://www.clarkcountynv.gov/government/elected_officials/county_treasurer/real-property-tax-information | verified: 2026-07-25].

## 7. SID and LID assessments

### 7a. What they are

A special assessment is "a charge levied against properties within the boundaries of an area known as a Special Improvement District (SID)." Typical improvements include "streets, sidewalks, curbs and gutters, streetlights, sewer and water facilities, etc." [source: https://www.clarkcountynv.gov/government/elected_officials/county_treasurer/understanding-sids | verified: 2026-07-25].

The cities use the same idea under different names. Clark County Public Works describes SIDs as a mechanism for "acquiring, improving, equipping, operating, and maintaining specific projects" [source: https://www.clarkcountynv.gov/government/departments/public_works_department/programs_and_services/special_improvement_districts.php | verified: 2026-07-25]. In Las Vegas and Henderson you will also see "Local Improvement District," "Special Assessment District" and "Maintenance District."

**Why this matters for new construction specifically.** SIDs are how the infrastructure in a new master-planned community got paid for. New communities are precisely where SIDs are live and unamortized. A resale home in an older neighborhood often has a matured district. A brand new Summerlin, Skye Canyon, Sunstone, Inspirada or Valley Vista home very often does not.

### 7b. How they are formed and how long they run

Clark County forms SIDs three ways: the Provisional Order Method (government-initiated, requires a public protest hearing), the Petition Method (owner-initiated, requires a protest hearing and majority frontage vote if the county does not fund 50 percent), and the **Developer Method**, negotiated between developers and the government with **no protest hearing required** [source: https://www.clarkcountynv.gov/government/departments/public_works_department/programs_and_services/special_improvement_districts.php | verified: 2026-07-25].

Nearly every new-community SID is the developer method. The buyer had no vote and no hearing. The obligation was attached to the lot before the lot was ever sold.

SIDs typically finance improvements "over a 10 year - up to a 30 year period at a low rate of interest," and the full process from proposal to bond sale can take up to two years [source: https://www.clarkcountynv.gov/government/departments/public_works_department/programs_and_services/special_improvement_districts.php | verified: 2026-07-25].

### 7c. How they are billed

Clark County: assessments are "typically billed and collected semi-annually" [source: https://www.clarkcountynv.gov/government/elected_officials/county_treasurer/understanding-sids | verified: 2026-07-25].

**They are billed separately from the property tax bill, and they are usually not in the mortgage escrow.** Many buyers do not realize a second bill exists until it arrives.

Assessment Management Group (AMG) administers billing for most valley districts, handling "Installment Billings, Communications with Property Owners, Delinquent Billings, Payoffs, Lien Releases... Title Company Communications, Mortgage Company Communications, Tax Service Coordination" [source: https://www.amgnv.com/improvementdistricts.asp | verified: 2026-07-25].

**Delinquency is serious.** "Within 60 days of a delinquency by the property owner, the County commences foreclosure proceedings to collect the outstanding debt," and late penalties are described as "substantial" [source: https://www.clarkcountynv.gov/government/elected_officials/county_treasurer/understanding-sids | verified: 2026-07-25].

**A closing-timing trap worth putting in the guide.** AMG's own notice states that after a deed is recorded it may take the Assessor approximately 15 days to change the ownership and mailing address, and "for any closing occurring within 15 days... prior to the 'Billing Date', payment should be paid through escrow directly to the proper mailing address" [source: https://www.amgnv.com/PDF/importantdates.pdf | verified: 2026-07-25]. Translation: if you close right before a billing date, the bill may go to the builder's old address and you will never see it. Ask escrow to handle it.

### 7e. Prepayment

Clark County's Treasurer page does not address prepayment or prepayment penalties [source: https://www.clarkcountynv.gov/government/elected_officials/county_treasurer/understanding-sids | verified: 2026-07-25]. AMG lists "Payoffs" among the services it administers [source: https://www.amgnv.com/improvementdistricts.asp | verified: 2026-07-25], so payoffs exist as a process.

**Typical prepayment penalty terms: NOT FOUND from an official source.** A secondary source describes penalties ranging from 3 percent down to 0 percent over the life of the bonds depending on the district. That is unverified. **Do not publish a penalty percentage.** Tell the reader to request a written payoff quote from AMG for the specific district.

**Typical annual assessment dollar amounts: NOT FOUND from an official source.** A secondary source cites $300 to $3,200 per home per year in 2026 depending on the master plan. That is unverified and should not be printed as fact. If the guide wants a range, it must be attributed as an estimate from a non-government source, or omitted.

### 7f. How a buyer finds out BEFORE signing

Give the reader this exact sequence. This is the actionable part.

1. **Get the assessor parcel number (APN) for the specific lot,** not the model home, not the community. Assessments attach to parcels.
2. **Search the parcel at AMG.** Clark County directs owners to search the Assessment Management Group site at amgnv.com for parcel information [source: https://www.clarkcountynv.gov/government/elected_officials/county_treasurer/understanding-sids | verified: 2026-07-25]. AMG's parcel search accepts parcel number, owner name or street name and covers Clark County, City of Las Vegas, City of North Las Vegas, City of Henderson and other jurisdictions [source: https://amgnv.com/parcelsearch_non_pop1.asp | verified: 2026-07-25].
3. **Ask the builder's sales office in writing:** "Is this lot in a SID or LID? What is the current annual assessment? When does it mature? What is the payoff balance today?" Get the answer on paper.
4. **Ask escrow and title for the assessment status** during the title review period. Title companies communicate with AMG as a matter of routine [source: https://www.amgnv.com/improvementdistricts.asp | verified: 2026-07-25].
5. **Call Clark County Public Works at (702) 455-6000** for unincorporated county parcels [source: https://www.clarkcountynv.gov/government/departments/public_works_department/programs_and_services/special_improvement_districts.php | verified: 2026-07-25], or **AMG at (702) 796-0082** for billing questions [source: https://www.amgnv.com/PDF/importantdates.pdf | verified: 2026-07-25].
6. **Add the assessment to the monthly budget** before deciding what house to buy. It is usually not in the mortgage payment.

---

## 8. Homeowners insurance in the Las Vegas valley

### 8a. What a policy covers and does not cover

The Nevada Division of Insurance explains that homeowners policies "combine various types of protections, like property damage, contents coverage, liability, medical payments, and temporary living expenses," and that "Standard excluded loss types such as flood, earthquake, and war require special insurance policies or special endorsements" [source: https://doi.nv.gov/Consumers/Homeowners-Insurance/ | verified: 2026-07-25].

**Flood is not covered by a standard homeowners policy.** That matters in the valley. Las Vegas gets very little total rainfall but has serious monsoon flash flooding, and new communities on the outskirts sit in and near washes. A buyer should check the flood zone for the specific lot and price a separate flood policy if needed.

### 8b. What drives the premium

Nevada DOI states insurers assess "risk factors, such as proximity to a fire house, burglar alarms, proximity to flood zones or earthquake faults and age of home," and that premiums reflect "the cost to replace or rebuild the house in the event of a total loss" [source: https://doi.nv.gov/Consumers/Homeowners-Insurance/ | verified: 2026-07-25].

The Division offers a Homeowner Coverage Tool for comparing companies [source: https://doi.nv.gov/Consumers/Homeowners-Insurance/ | verified: 2026-07-25]. That is a free, neutral shopping resource and is worth naming in the guide.

### 8c. New-construction specifics

Points that follow logically from the DOI's own stated rating factors, framed as questions for the buyer rather than as claims:

- **The policy is rated on rebuild cost, not purchase price.** On a new build, purchase price includes the lot, the builder's margin and any SID-funded infrastructure. Rebuild cost is the structure only. Ask the agent to insure to replacement cost, not to the sales price.
- **Age of home is a rating factor** and a brand new home is the best possible answer to it. New roof, new wiring, new plumbing, current code. Ask whether the carrier gives a new-home or new-roof credit.
- **Proximity to a fire station is a rating factor.** New communities on the valley's edge can be farther from a station than established neighborhoods. Worth checking before choosing between two communities.
- **Design center upgrades change the rebuild number.** A buyer who adds $80,000 of upgrades should tell the insurance agent, or be underinsured on day one.
- **Coverage must be bound before closing** and the first year premium is usually paid at closing as a prepaid item.

### 8d. Average cost figures

**Verified Clark County or Las Vegas average homeowners premium for 2026: NOT FOUND from a government or NAIC primary source.** Third-party comparison sites reported Las Vegas averages ranging from roughly $1,393 to roughly $1,713 per year in 2026, and those sources disagree with each other. Those are marketing sites with an incentive to show low numbers. **Do not print an average premium in the guide.** Tell the reader to get real quotes on the specific address, and point them at the Nevada DOI Homeowner Coverage Tool.

NAIC publishes a national Homeowners Insurance Report with state-level average premium by policy form, but the most recent edition located in this pass covered 2022 data [source: https://content.naic.org/sites/default/files/publication-hmr-zu-homeowners-report.pdf | verified: 2026-07-25]. That is four years stale and should not be presented as current.

The full statewide tables (Mineral, Storey, Washoe and the other counties) were not carried into this file except where the official page publishes only a statewide range and no Clark County figure exists, which is disclosed as such in section 2c.
